title: Grade 3 Math — Thu, Jun 26
description: Fractions — Day 4 of 5: Simple addition of like fractions
subject: mathematics

questions.explanation: Adding like fractions: keep the denominator, add numerators. 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4.

questions.question: Anita ate 2/8 of a watermelon and Ravi ate 3/8. How much did they eat together?
What is the rule for adding like fractions?
options: Add both numerators and both denominators
Keep the denominator; add only the numerators
Multiply the numerators; keep the denominator
questions.explanation: When adding like fractions: keep the common denominator unchanged and add only the numerators. Example: 2/5 + 3/5 = (2+3)/5 = 5/5.

questions.question: 1/3 + 1/3 = ? What does this equal as a simpler fraction?
questions.explanation: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3. Two one-thirds make two-thirds. No simplification needed here.

questions.question: Ritu completed 3/10 of her project on Monday and 4/10 on Tuesday. What fraction has she completed so far?
questions.explanation: 3/10 + 4/10 = 7/10. She has completed seven-tenths of her project.

questions.question: What happens when the sum of like fractions equals the denominator (like 4/4)?
options: It is an improper fraction we ignore
questions.explanation: When numerator = denominator, the fraction equals 1 (one whole). Example: 3/3 = 1, 4/4 = 1, 7/7 = 1.

questions.question: A bucket was 2/9 full. Sonu poured more water to make it 6/9 full. How much water did he add?
questions.explanation: He added: 6/9 − 2/9 = 4/9. (This is a subtraction problem using the addition context.)

questions.question: Aman has done 2/8 of his homework. He needs to complete it fully. How much is left?
Is 2/5 + 3/5 + 2/5 possible? What is the answer?
options: Not possible — only two like fractions can be added
questions.explanation: You can add three or more like fractions. 2/5 + 3/5 + 2/5 = 7/5. This is more than 1 whole (improper fraction), and that's perfectly valid.

questions.question: Class quiz: 3 students answered 1/6, 2/6 and 2/6 of the questions correctly. What fraction of questions did all three get right?
questions.explanation: 1/6 + 2/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Together they answered five-sixths of the questions correctly.

questions.question: Why can't you add 2/3 and 3/5 using the same rule as like fractions?
options: Because fractions can never be added
Because denominators are different — you need to find a common denominator first
Because 3 and 5 are both odd numbers
questions.explanation: 2/3 and 3/5 have different denominators (unlike fractions). To add them, you must first convert to a common denominator. The like-fraction rule only works when denominators are already the same.
